text: Here are the anchors worth keeping. This appendix is your lookup manual -- use Ctrl+G (Go to Line) or Ctrl+Shift+O (Go to Symbol) to jump directly to a setting name. text: Put 3. Accessible Diff Viewer - Complete Guide into plain language. The Accessible Diff Viewer presents file diffs as a structured, line-by-line list instead of a visual side-by-side view.

speaker: ALEX
text: A solid pull request habit is to separate three questions: what changed, why it changed, and what still needs review. That keeps the conversation useful instead of noisy.

text: When to Use Accessible Diff Viewer.

speaker: ALEX
text: These are the details that keep the idea from floating away. Reviewing pull request changes. Resolving merge conflicts. Comparing file versions (Timeline view). Reviewing Copilot-generated edits. Any time you need to understand what changed in a file.

speaker: ALEX
text: Before the learner moves on. The Accessible Diff Viewer starts with a header showing the file path and change summary. It then shows each hunk (changed section) in order.

text: Start here: Open Settings: Ctrl+,. Then: Search: "diffEditor.renderSideBySide". Next: Uncheck the box (or set to false in settings.json).

speaker: ALEX
text: Hold that next to this. Learning Cards: Accessible Diff Viewer.

speaker: ALEX
text: Press F7 in any diff editor to jump to the first changed hunk -- then F7 / Shift+F7 to move between hunks. Use Alt+F2 (Accessible View) to read the full diff in a structured, non-streaming pane with proper line prefixes. Switch to inline diff view (diffEditor.renderSideBySide: false) so all changes appear in one editor instead of two panels. Inline diff view places removed and added lines back-to-back with color-coded backgrounds -- increase font size for easier scanning. Enable accessibility.signals.diffLineInserted and diffLineDeleted for audio feedback as you arrow through changed lines. Zoom the diff editor independently with Ctrl+= if the surrounding UI is already at a comfortable size.

speaker: ALEX
text: For a learner, the useful signals are concrete. NVDA Menu → Preferences → Settings → Browse Mode. "Maximum length of text on a single line": 10000. "Automatic focus mode for focus changes": Checked. "Automatic focus mode for caret movement": Unchecked. "Report tooltips": Unchecked (reduces interruptions; use Alt+F2 instead). "Report notifications": Checked.

speaker: ALEX
text: Think of this as 4 checks: Browse Mode settings; Object Presentation; Speech settings; and Input Composition.

speaker: ALEX
text: That connects to another useful point. NVDA add-ons for VS Code.

speaker: ALEX
text: Focus Highlight - shows focus location visually (helpful for sighted trainers). IndentNav - navigate by indentation level (useful for Python, YAML).

"Report tooltip text": Unchecked (use Alt+F2 instead). "Punctuation Level": Most (for code). "Speak Long Lines Continuously": Yes. "Blank Line Announcement": Tone (less verbose than speech).

speaker: ALEX
text: control how much information VS Code announces. Verbose: Announces full context and details minimal: Announces only essential information off: No automatic announcements (use Accessible View manually).

text: Let's pause on Signal Priorities. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: When multiple signals occur simultaneously, VS Code prioritizes them. This prevents overlapping announcements.

speaker: ALEX
text: Think of this as 4 checks: Errors (highest priority) - always announced; Warnings - announced after errors; Completions - announced if no errors/warnings; and Focus changes - announced last.

speaker: ALEX
text: Put that beside the next piece. Learning Cards: Accessibility Signals.

speaker: ALEX
text: Listen for the small confirmations in this list. Start with auto for most signals -- they play only when screen reader mode is active, keeping things quiet otherwise. The lineHasError and taskFailed signals are the highest-value audio cues; enable these first. Use accessibility.signals.volume (0-100) to balance signal volume against your screen reader speech. Audio cues supplement visual indicators you might miss -- enable lineHasWarning and lineHasError for sounds on the current line. The save and format signals confirm file operations completed without needing to check the status bar visually. Pair audio cues with high-contrast gutter icons for a dual-channel (sight + sound) feedback loop.
